cards.question: What is an array?
cards.answer: An array is a data structure that stores a fixed-size, ordered collection of elements, typically of the same type, in contiguous memory locations. Each element is accessed by its numeric index.

cards.question: Why do arrays offer O(1) random access?
cards.answer: Because elements are stored contiguously, the address of element i is computed as base_address + i * element_size. This arithmetic takes constant time regardless of array size.

cards.question: What is the time complexity of inserting an element at the beginning or middle of an array?
cards.answer: O(n), because subsequent elements must be shifted one position to make room. Inserting at the end (when capacity exists) is O(1).

cards.question: What is the time complexity of deleting an element from an array at index i?
cards.answer: O(n) in general, since elements after index i must be shifted left to fill the gap. Deleting the last element is O(1).

cards.question: What is the time complexity of searching in an unsorted array versus a sorted array?
cards.answer: Unsorted: O(n) using linear search. Sorted: O(log n) using binary search.

cards.question: What is the difference between a static array and a dynamic array?
cards.answer: A static array has a fixed size set at creation, while a dynamic array (e.g., Python list, Java ArrayList, C++ vector) can grow or shrink automatically. Dynamic arrays resize by allocating a larger block and copying elements over.

cards.question: Why is appending to a dynamic array amortized O(1)?
cards.answer: When full, the array typically doubles its capacity, an O(n) copy that happens rarely. Spread across many appends, the average cost per append is constant.

cards.question: How are arrays indexed in most programming languages, and what happens with out-of-bounds access?
cards.answer: Most languages use zero-based indexing, so valid indices are 0 to n-1. Out-of-bounds access raises an error in safe languages (e.g., IndexError, ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException) but causes undefined behavior in C/C++.

cards.question: What are the main advantages and disadvantages of arrays?
cards.answer: Advantages: fast index access, cache-friendly contiguous memory, low overhead. Disadvantages: fixed size (for static arrays), costly insertions/deletions in the middle, and need for contiguous memory.

cards.question: How is a multidimensional (2D) array stored in memory?
cards.answer: It is flattened into one contiguous block, either in row-major order (rows stored consecutively, as in C) or column-major order (columns stored consecutively, as in Fortran). In row-major, element [i][j] is at i * num_cols + j.

cards.question: Why are arrays considered cache-friendly?
cards.answer: Contiguous storage means that accessing one element loads neighboring elements into the CPU cache, giving good spatial locality. Sequential traversal is therefore very fast compared to pointer-based structures like linked lists.

cards.question: How does an array compare to a linked list in terms of access and insertion?
cards.answer: Arrays offer O(1) index access but O(n) insertion/deletion in the middle, while linked lists have O(n) access but O(1) insertion/deletion once the position is known. Arrays also use less memory per element since they don't store pointers.
